# Configuration, constants and errors {#sec-config-errors}

This page documents two small modules that are used by every other module, and
the exception hierarchy: `backend/core/config.py`, `backend/core/constants.py`
and `backend/core/errors.py`.

## The two constant modules {.unnumbered}

The values are split into two files, because they have two different meanings.

| File | Contents | May be changed? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `constants.py` | Mathematical and structural constants. | **No.** They are part of the definition of the project. |
| `config.py` | Policy parameters. | **Yes.** They describe a choice, not a law. |

Both are imported as modules.

```python
from backend.core import config, constants

limit = config.MAX_QUBITS
turn = constants.TWO_PI
```

## The fixed constants (`constants.py`) {.unnumbered}

| Constant | Value | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `TWO_PI` | `2 * pi` | One full turn, in radians. It is used for the turns-to-radians conversion. |
| `NATIVE_OPS` | tuple | The names of the allowed native operations: `gpi`, `gpi2`, `ms`, `zz` and `virtual_z`. |

These values never change. They are not configuration.

## The tunable parameters (`config.py`) {.unnumbered}

| Parameter | Value | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MAX_QUBITS` | `28` | The hard cap on the circuit width. |
| `MAX_STEPS_WARNING` | `500` | If more steps than this are produced, a warning is logged. |
| `VIBRATION_THRESHOLD` | `0.01` | The smallest per-qubit error that is reported as vibration. |
| `JSON_DECIMALS` | `6` | The number of decimals used when a floating-point number is written. |

### How the width limit is used {.unnumbered}

The limit is not taken from `MAX_QUBITS` alone. The backend is also asked for
its own number of qubits. The effective limit is the smaller of the two.

- The cap is `MAX_QUBITS`, which is 28.
- When the backend exposes a `num_qubits` attribute with a positive integer, the
  effective limit is `min(MAX_QUBITS, backend.num_qubits)`.
- When the backend does not expose it, the cap of 28 is used.

In this way, a circuit is never sent to a backend that is too small for it. For
example, a 26-qubit circuit is rejected by an Aria backend, which has 25 qubits.

The check is made in `transpiler._effective_max_qubits`, at the start of the
pipeline.

## The error module {.unnumbered}

The file `backend/core/errors.py` defines a small hierarchy of exceptions. Only
these exceptions are raised by the backend, so that a caller can catch all the
expected failures with one `except` clause.

```
QVizError
├── UnsupportedOperationError
├── CircuitTooLargeError
└── TranspilationError
```

| Exception | Raised when |
| --- | --- |
| `QVizError` | The base class. It is not raised directly. It is used to catch any QViz error. |
| `UnsupportedOperationError` | The circuit contains an operation that cannot be shown, for example a mid-circuit measurement, a `reset`, or classical control flow. |
| `CircuitTooLargeError` | The circuit is wider than the effective limit that is described above. |
| `TranspilationError` | The circuit could not be transpiled for the chosen backend. |

### An unknown provider is not an error {.unnumbered}

If the provider of a backend cannot be recognised, no error is raised. The
backend is handled by a generic strategy instead. This behaviour is described on
the [Provider](provider.qmd) page. An error is raised only when an operation has
no meaning in a visualiser.
